content: Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) is a persistent inflammatory condition of the middle ear and mastoid cavity, often caused by multiple microorganisms. It is characterized by ear discharge (otorrhoea) through a perforated eardrum and is commonly associated with hearing loss. Aural toileting refers to various manual ear-cleaning techniques, including dry mopping (using cotton wool or tissue), suction clearance (often performed under a microscope), and irrigation (using syringes, either manually or automatically). Dry mopping can effectively remove mucopurulent discharge but is less effective than suction or irrigation in clearing epithelial debris or thick pus. Aural toileting can be used as a standalone treatment or in combination with other therapies, such as antibiotics or topical antiseptics. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of aural toileting procedures in managing CSOM. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including Cochrane ENT Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, up to March 16, 2020. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with at least one week of follow-up were included. Participants were adults or children with chronic ear discharge lasting more than two weeks, either due to CSOM or an unknown cause. The interventions studied included any method of aural toileting, compared to either no intervention, placebo, or other aural toileting methods. Background treatments, such as topical antibiotics or antiseptics, were used in both study arms when applicable. The primary outcomes assessed were the resolution of ear discharge (measured at various time points), health-related quality of life, and ear pain or discomfort. Secondary outcomes included hearing, serious complications, and adverse events such as ear bleeding, dizziness, vertigo, or balance problems. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Three studies involving 431 participants (465 ears) were included. Two studies focused on children with CSOM in community settings (351 participants), while the third study included both children and adults with chronic ear discharge lasting at least six weeks (80 participants). None of the studies reported outcomes related to health-related quality of life, ear pain, or ear bleeding as an adverse event. Daily aural toileting (dry mopping) versus no treatment: Two studies (351 children; 370 ears) compared daily dry mopping with no treatment. Neither study provided data on the resolution of ear discharge at one to two weeks or two to four weeks. For resolution of ear discharge after four weeks, one study reported results per person. However, the evidence was of very low certainty, and it remains unclear whether there is any difference between the groups at 16 weeks (risk ratio [RR] 1.01, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.60 to 1.72; 1 study; 217 participants). No data were reported on adverse events such as dizziness, vertigo, or balance problems. One study mentioned serious complications but did not specify which group these complications occurred in or whether they were preor post-treatment. Hearing outcomes were reported in one study, but the results were presented by treatment outcome rather than by treatment group, making it impossible to determine differences between the groups. Daily aural toileting versus single aural toileting combined with topical ciprofloxacin: One study (80 participants; 95 ears) compared daily aural toileting (suction) combined with clinic-administered topical ciprofloxacin ear drops to a single episode of aural toileting (suction) followed by self-administered daily topical ciprofloxacin ear drops. The evidence was of very low certainty, and it is unclear whether there is a difference in the resolution of ear discharge at one to two weeks (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.30; 1 study; 80 participants). No data were available for the resolution of ear discharge at two to four weeks. For resolution of ear discharge after four weeks, results were reported by ear rather than by person, making it difficult to interpret. One participant in the single aural toileting group reported dizziness, which the authors attributed to the use of cold ciprofloxacin drops. The evidence was very uncertain regarding differences between the groups for this adverse event (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.95; 1 study; 80 participants). No data were reported for other adverse events, such as vertigo or balance problems, or for serious complications. Hearing outcomes were only reported qualitatively, with the authors stating there was no difference between the groups, but the certainty of this evidence was very low. Conclusions: The evidence regarding the effectiveness of aural toileting in resolving ear discharge in people with CSOM is highly uncertain due to a lack of data and the poor quality of available studies. Similarly, there is significant uncertainty about other outcomes, including adverse events, as these were not well reported. It is also unclear whether daily suction clearance followed by clinic-administered antibiotic ear drops is superior to a single suction episode followed by self-administered topical antibiotic drops.
